common_name: Chicago Blackout Daylily (Deep Near-Black Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; part of the influential Chicago series of daylilies bred by Earl Hall.

directions: Chicago Blackout bears richly saturated, near-black red flowers, one of the darkest reds among the many well-regarded Chicago-series daylilies bred by Earl Hall, a lineage that also produced the widely grown Chicago Apache and Chicago Fire. The dramatic dark color reads best against light-colored companion plants or pale groundcovers, where the depth of the red-black petals stands out rather than disappearing into shadow. Well-branched scapes hold the flowers above clumping grassy foliage through a solid midsummer season. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Eenie Weenie Daylily (Classic Miniature Clear Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a long-popular miniature daylily grown for its tidy habit and heavy, reliable bloom.

directions: Eenie Weenie produces a steady, heavy succession of small, clear yellow flowers on a compact, low-growing plant, one of the classic older miniature daylilies still popular for edging a border or filling a small garden space where full-sized daylily clumps would be out of scale. Its tidy, grassy foliage stays neat through the season, and the sheer number of blooms produced per scape makes it a dependable, low-maintenance choice. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, since vigorous miniatures like this one can become root-bound faster than larger cultivars.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Little Wine Cup Daylily (Miniature Wine-Red Cup-Shaped Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; a compact miniature daylily with rounded, cup-shaped flowers.

directions: Little Wine Cup bears small, rounded, cup-shaped flowers in a deep wine-red, held on well-branched scapes above a compact clump of grassy foliage. Its miniature scale and rich, saturated color make it a good choice for the front of a mixed perennial border or a container planting where a larger-flowered daylily would look out of proportion. It blooms heavily over the midsummer season and increases at a steady, manageable rate. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom count high.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Betty Warren Woods Daylily (Large Ruffled Cream Exhibition Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; a popular exhibition-quality cultivar known for its large, heavily ruffled flowers.

directions: Betty Warren Woods bears very large, near-white to pale cream flowers with heavily ruffled, substantial petals and a subtle green throat, a combination of size and texture that has made it a long-standing favorite on the daylily show table as well as in the garden. Well-branched scapes hold the huge blooms upright without flopping, an important trait given the flower's exceptional size. The pale, neutral color combines easily with almost any other daylily or perennial nearby. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, feed lightly in spring to support the large flower size, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Chicago Royal Robe Daylily (Deep Purple-Violet Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; part of the influential Chicago series of daylilies bred by Earl Hall.

directions: Chicago Royal Robe bears deep purple-violet flowers with a lighter throat, part of the extensive Chicago series bred by Earl Hall that also produced the well-known Chicago Apache and Chicago Fire, this time exploring the cooler end of the color range instead of the series' famous reds and oranges. Well-branched scapes hold flowers above a vigorous clump of grassy foliage through the midsummer season. Its rich, regal purple tone combines well with yellow- or gold-flowered companion daylilies for strong color contrast in a mixed bed. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

directions: Buttermint bears small, rounded, pale butter-yellow flowers held on well-branched scapes above a modest grassy clump, a soft, easygoing color that blends into almost any planting scheme without competing for attention. Its smaller flower size and moderate height suit a mixed perennial border or a mass planting along a walkway better than a large-flowered exhibition-type daylily. It blooms heavily and dependably through the midsummer season with minimal care. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom production strong.

common_name: Neyron Rose Daylily (Historic Clear Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; an older cultivar that helped establish clear pink as an achievable daylily color decades ago.

directions: Neyron Rose bears clear, true pink flowers with a lightly ruffled edge, an older cultivar from the era when breeding pink out of the daylily's naturally orange- and yellow-dominated palette was still a novel achievement, and it has been kept in circulation for its clean, uncomplicated color ever since. Well-branched scapes hold the flowers above a vigorous clump of grassy foliage through the midsummer season. Its straightforward pink combines easily with nearly any other daylily color in a mixed border. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Golden Chimes Daylily (Historic Small Bell-Shaped Golden-Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; a mid-twentieth-century heirloom daylily still valued for its graceful, small bell-shaped flowers and heavy branching.

directions: Golden Chimes bears small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in a warm golden yellow with mahogany-brown reverse petal backs, produced in exceptionally heavy numbers on well-branched, wiry scapes that give the plant a graceful, airy look quite different from the bold, flat-faced flowers of most modern hybrid daylilies. Introduced in the 1950s, it has remained popular for its historic significance and its still-impressive floriferousness even next to far newer cultivars. Its smaller, dainty flowers work especially well massed in a naturalistic planting or along a sunny slope. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain strong bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database

common_name: Fragrant Returns Daylily (Reblooming Fragrant Pale Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; a popular reblooming, richly fragrant small-flowered daylily bred in the tradition of the Happy Returns and Rosy Returns series.

directions: Fragrant Returns bears pale lemon-yellow flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance noticeable from several feet away, a trait bred deliberately into this compact rebloomer since most daylilies have little to no scent. Like its relatives Happy Returns and Rosy Returns, it flowers over an extended season from early summer through fall on a compact, tidy plant well suited to the front of a border or mass planting along a walkway where its fragrance can be appreciated up close. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the heavy, extended bloom production going strong.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Cultivar Registration Database
